title_original: Scientific computing in the age of agentic AI
description: A new field report shows how scientists use AI coding agents to modernize scientific computing, accelerating software development and discovery in genomics and beyond.
title_he: Scientific computing in the age of agentic AI
summary_he: Research teams are leveraging AI agents to modernize scientific software, enabling them to focus on discovery rather than tedious implementation tasks. By automating engineering work, AI agents accelerate software development and maintenance, but also raise challenges in establishing long-term responsibility and stewardship.
details_he: The use of AI agents in scientific computing is transforming the field by allowing researchers to prototype ideas more quickly and pursue projects that were previously impractical. Agents are helping to modernize scientific software, making it more efficient and better maintained. However, this shift also requires a change in the researchers' role, from implementation to verification and orchestration. While AI agents provide velocity uplift, expert guidance and understanding are still necessary to ensure the quality and scientific direction of the resulting tools.

title_he: Cato CTRL™ Threat Research: SilverFox Evolves: Abuse of New Drivers and Trusted Software Hijacking Enable Remote Access with ValleyRAT in Japan
summary_he: SilverFox, a threat group, has expanded its toolkit by combining new tactics such as vulnerable-driver abuse, DLL sideloading, and layered recovery mechanisms to maintain execution of ValleyRAT in a Japanese industrial manufacturing sector organization.
details_he: The attack began with a phishing lure in the form of an invoice, using legitimate QQ and Tencent Cloud services to host attacker-controlled content. The attackers then abused ConvertToPDF.exe and PDFDirect.exe to sideload a malicious PDFCORE8.dll, which embedded three vulnerable drivers: BootRepair.sys, EnPortv.sys, and wsftprm.sys. The malware integrated various techniques to impair security controls and maintain execution, including Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), DLL sideloading, NTDLL unhooking, and process injection.

title_original: Your AI Governance Policy Should Survive Your Next Model Change
description: The model migration is ready for approval. Tests show better performance and lower costs. The application will serve the same users, process the same data, and support the same business workflow. The product team expects a straightforward technical sign-off. Then security asks the question that changes the review: which controls will survive the switch? Access rules, data protection, logging, and human approval may depend on settings provided by the current model platform. A migration can alter the organization’s effective policy even when the business use stays exactly the same. Models and providers will keep changing. The requirements attached to business […]The postYour AI Governance Policy Should Survive Your Next Model Changeappeared first onCheck Point Blog.
title_he: Your AI Governance Policy Should Survive Your Next Model Change
summary_he: AI governance policies must be adaptable to accommodate changes in AI models and platforms, ensuring consistent application of rules across different implementations.
details_he: The increasing use of multiple AI models and platforms by enterprises creates challenges for AI governance, as each new model, tool, or interface requires teams to interpret and apply the organization's policy. This can lead to governance drift, where the practical meaning of the policy changes from one implementation to the next. To address this, organizations should make the use case the anchor for governance, defining the requirements that should travel with the use case, such as identity and accountability, permitted purpose, data protection, logging, and human approval. This approach ensures that the governance policy remains consistent and effective, even as the underlying model changes.
